To fix (5)

To fix Ethics Approval Check

What we found

1 of 1 paper appeared to involve live data collection and lacked an ethics approval statement.

Show details

Based on the following text, we would expect an ethics approval statement, but it was not present:

We recruited 200 participants through Prolific (50% female, 42% White, 36 years old on average).

Procedure Participants were given some examples of asymmetries of analogical directions (outside of the base and target domains).

Thus, we recruited 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).

After a brief introduction to the task (slightly varied from Study 1 to ensure robustness), participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials.

Participants were simply asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.

After completing all 12 trials and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.

Thus, we recruited 200 participants on Prolific (50% female, 46% White, 36 years on average).

Participants were given a refresher of what an analogy is, and an example (the Bohr model of the atom).

Given our design, this required the recruitment of 300 total participants on Prolific (50% female, 52% White, 37 years on average).

Participants were given 6 comparison trials and 6 filler trials, where they were asked which analogy was better on a 7-point Likert scale.

After completing all 12 trials (which were randomized), and an attention check, participants were thanked for their time and compensated.

We observed this asymmetry when comparing the best analogies in either direction (Study 1), when we randomly paired bases and targets in either direction (Study 2), and when participants were asked to generate their own analogies (Study 3).

Finally, our participants were recruited largely from wealthy, English speaking nations.

Participants who failed our preregistered attention check were excluded from the analysis (n = 7).

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen’s d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

To fix Exact P-Values

What we found

We found 1 imprecise p value out of 27 detected p values.

Show details

Reporting p values imprecisely (e.g., p < .05) reduces transparency, reproducibility, and re-use (e.g., in p value meta-analyses). Best practice is to report exact p-values with three decimal places (e.g., p = .032) unless p values are smaller than 0.001, in which case you can use p < .001.

This module sometimes flags false positives when sentences discuss how p-value thresholds were set. It can also miss an imprecise p-value that is reported against a threshold (e.g., “decreased at the p < .05 significance threshold”).

P-Value Text
p’s > 0.07 There was no difference between analogies with the physical mechanical base in length and word frequency compared to the other domains (p’s > 0.07) and as before, including length and frequency as covariates for the analogies did not change the significance of any effects.

The APA manual states: Report exact p values (e.g., p = .031) to two or three decimal places. However, report p values less than .001 as p < .001. However, 2 decimals is too imprecise for many use-cases (e.g., a p value meta-analysis), so report p values with three digits.

American Psychological Association (2020). Publication manual of the American Psychological Association, 7 edition. American Psychological Association.

To check Non-Significant P Value Check

What we found

We found 12 non-significant p values that should be checked for appropriate interpretation.

Show details

Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is ‘no effect’, ‘no difference’, or that groups are ‘the same’ after p > 0.05.

It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is ‘not significantly’ different, although this just restates that p > 0.05.

Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values.

Code Comments

Best programming practice is to add comments to code, to explain what the code does (to yourself in the future, or peers who want to re-use your code).

Missing Files

All files loaded in the code were present in the repository.

Absolute Paths

Best programming practice is to use relative file paths (e.g., ‘./files’) instead of absolute file paths (e.g., ‘C://Lakens/project_dir/files’) as these folder names do not exist on other computers. No absolute file paths were found in any of the code files.

Working Directory (setwd)

Best programming practice is to avoid setwd() in analysis code: it hardcodes an assumption about the working directory (often an absolute path on the author’s own machine), so the code breaks when run anywhere else. Keep the working directory as the caller sets it and use relative paths. No setwd() calls were found in any of the code files.

Package Installation (install.packages)

Best programming practice is to avoid install.packages() in analysis code: it installs software on whoever runs the script without asking, which is at minimum disruptive (an unexpected install, network access, a package version the author never tested against) and at worst a security risk if it points at an untrusted repository. Document required packages instead (a README, or a list of them: an renv.lock/DESCRIPTION for R, a requirements.txt for Python). No install.packages() calls were found in any of the code files.

Libraries / Imports

Best programming practice is to load all required libraries/imports in one block near the top of the code. In all code files, libraries/imports were loaded in one block.

Packages / Dependencies

The code files load 10 distinct packages/libraries: broom.mixed, emmeans, LexOPS, lmerTest, patchwork, ragg, stringi, systemfonts, tidytext, tidyverse. These are the names found in the source (no version information is available from static analysis).

Reproducible Environment

No renv.lock file, sessionInfo()/session_info() record, or groundhog/checkpoint date-pin call was found anywhere in the repository. Without one of these, the exact R and package versions used for the analysis are not recoverable, and package versions may drift between when this analysis was run and any later reproduction attempt. Consider depositing an renv.lock (via the renv package), a sessionInfo() text dump, or a groundhog/checkpoint date-pin alongside the code.

Parsable code

All R-type code files (.R, .Rmd, .qmd) could be read in. There were no parsing issues.

6a05b716ea7bab7464d2f818 Life is like an elevator it goes up and down mech
546e2f3cfdf99b2bc7ebcfe5 Emotion regulation is like riding a bicycle. You learn as you go and realize things as time goes on. It’s all about practice. mech
5d190e1c686b190018ea4d86 Motivation is like the ticking of a clock, you can go round and round and not really feel like you’re getting anywhere and then, all of a sudden, it’s time, time to get up and go get it. mech
668160122d968e44eb1bffbe Emotion regulation is like a washing machine - it runs in cycles - some gentle, some spinning out control. mech
55bb9ae7fdf99b26d27fda01 A clock is like memory, it only lasts a moment in time. psych
69f20e3fc0f0999c5d26cf7a A clock is the same as motivation in terms of it’s ability to only move forward, no matter the outcome. Our motivation continually moves forward, like the hands on a clock, progressing onwards. mech
6a1eeb2e312b07bacb2698c0 Emotions are a lot like elevators. Emotions can go up and down. Elevators go up and down. mech
6671e630d492b149069c46c1 Like a clock where it tells time, your emotions, when in a heighten state, cannot be regulated properly if you do not realize the importance of how it can be affected in the long term. mech
5f8f436e4676a71879786b95 An elevator lifts you up to the level you want just like feeling happiness and joy lifts your emotions psych
69f63f5d0140c343cacf3e4a Decision making is much like choosing a floor once in an elevator. There are a set number of options but it is up to you which you take. Only one will lead you immediately to the correct destination. Others may get you there still but in a less direct route. mech
6a0a236e3eb9974e261b3345 Sometimes human memory functions like a washing machine - it spins around everything in your head, tangling events together. At the end, your conscious is clean from recalling unpleasant events, only a distant feeling of them remains - everything else is left neat and tidy. mech
5a5a4bc8e0cf3d0001267426 A washing machine can vary greatly in terms of power and efficiency. Sometimes they will do a simple wash but a more powerful machine can do much more including drying the load afterwards. Decisions are needed to be made on what programme to use and before this which machine is the best value for the purchaser psych
6a1d936d144dcea7a8d4f896 Motivation can increase and decrease, up and down, just like an elevator travelling to different floors. Sometimes it may stay on one floor for a while but it could change at any moment. mech
6a1ce5c1d9e845bd58b24a03 A clock is like motivation in the sense that time is always moving forward. psych
69d6a29aad0913f7e6776233 Motivation is like a car engine. It gets you started. You need the accelerator to actually move. You can start off motivated but it doesn’t sustain if you are not determined. mech
673a79d52880fa454ca618e2 Regulating emotions is a lot like operating an elevator. Sometimes when I’m upset, I need to find ways to take things down a notch (ride the elevator down). Sometimes I’m around people who upset me and I need to disengage (get in the elevator and close the door). Sometimes I just need a really long grounding pause (emergency stop). mech
60dd2116d964fd7ff2b9ed54 Emotion regulation is like an elevator. It will go up but it can always come back down. You just need to press the button mech

mp_1 mechanical vs psychological mechanical psychological A Spring as Expectation Under Tension Spring expectation A spring is like expectation under tension: the farther reality is displaced from what is expected, the stronger the psychological pressure to restore consistency. Likewise, stretching or compressing a spring creates a restoring force that increases with displacement.
mp_2 mechanical vs psychological mechanical psychological A Mechanical Ratchet as Commitment Ratchet commitment A mechanical ratchet is like commitment: each completed step becomes psychologically difficult to reverse, so progress accumulates in one direction. Likewise, a ratchet permits motion tooth by tooth while mechanically preventing backward motion.
mp_3 mechanical vs psychological mechanical psychological Mechanical Resonance as Emotional Triggering Resonance emotion Mechanical resonance is like emotional triggering: a small recurring stimulus can produce an unexpectedly large response when it matches an already sensitive psychological pattern. Likewise, repeated forces applied at a system’s natural frequency can build increasingly large mechanical oscillations.
mp_4 mechanical vs psychological mechanical psychological A Mechanical Governor as Self-Control Governor self-control A mechanical governor is like self-control: when behavior begins exceeding a desired level, an internal corrective process pushes it back toward a target. Likewise, a centrifugal governor automatically reduces a machine’s input when its rotational speed rises too far.
mp_5 mechanical vs psychological mechanical psychological A Flywheel as Psychological Momentum Flywheel momentum A flywheel is like psychological momentum: once a belief or intention is strongly established, it tends to keep thought moving in the same direction despite small disturbances. Likewise, a spinning flywheel stores rotational energy and resists sudden changes in speed.
mp_6 mechanical vs psychological mechanical psychological A Gear Train as a Chain of Reasoning Gear train reasoning A gear train is like a chain of reasoning: one thought constrains the next, transmitting an initial premise through a sequence of dependent transformations. Likewise, each gear transfers motion to the next, converting the original rotation into a predictable final motion.
pm_1 mechanical vs psychological psychological mechanical Attention as a Movable Spotlight Attention spotlight Attention is like a movable spotlight: it illuminates a narrow region of a larger field, making whatever falls inside it easier to inspect. Moving the beam toward one target necessarily leaves other targets in relative darkness.
pm_2 mechanical vs psychological psychological mechanical Cognitive Dissonance as a Misaligned Gear Train Dissonance gears Cognitive dissonance is like tension in a misaligned gear train: incompatible beliefs pull the system in directions that cannot smoothly coexist. The mind reduces the strain by adjusting, reinterpreting, or discarding one of the conflicting elements until the mechanism runs more smoothly.
pm_3 mechanical vs psychological psychological mechanical Emotion Regulation as a Pressure-Control Valve Emotion regulation valve Emotion regulation is like a pressure-control valve: emotional pressure can build inside the system, while regulatory processes determine how quickly and through which channels it is released. A valve that is too open produces uncontrolled discharge, while one that is too tightly shut allows pressure to accumulate.
pm_4 mechanical vs psychological psychological mechanical Habit as a Well-Worn Mechanical Track Habit track Habit is like a well-worn mechanical track: repeated movement deepens the channel until the system naturally follows the same path with little guidance. Changing the behavior requires either blocking the old track or repeatedly forcing motion along a new one.
pm_5 mechanical vs psychological psychological mechanical Working Memory as a Workbench Working memory workbench Working memory is like a workbench: only a few objects can be kept on its surface at once, while everything else must be stored elsewhere. Adding too many items causes interference, just as an overcrowded bench makes each task harder to perform.
pm_6 mechanical vs psychological psychological mechanical Self-Control as a Mechanical Governor Self-control governor Self-control is like a mechanical governor: it continuously detects when behavior is drifting away from a chosen target and applies corrective force. Strong self-control is therefore less like constant braking than like a well-tuned mechanism making small adjustments before large deviations occur.
be_1 filler (biological vs economic) biological economic Cellular Metabolism as a Production Economy NA NA Cellular metabolism is like a production economy: cells allocate scarce inputs such as glucose, oxygen, and amino acids across competing biochemical pathways to produce energy, structures, and waste. Bottlenecks in one input can constrain total output even when other resources are abundant.
be_2 filler (biological vs economic) biological economic Immune System as an Insurance Market NA NA The immune system is like an insurance market: it pays continuous costs to maintain defenses against uncertain future biological losses. Greater investment in surveillance and preparedness can reduce the expected damage from rare but costly infections.
be_3 filler (biological vs economic) biological economic Sexual Selection as an Auction Market NA NA Sexual selection is like an auction market: individuals compete for reproductive opportunities using costly signals, displays, or resources, while potential mates discriminate among the available bids. Traits can become increasingly elaborate when success depends on relative attractiveness rather than sheer survival value.
be_4 filler (biological vs economic) biological economic Food Web as a Supply Chain NA NA A food web is like a supply chain: energy and matter move through interconnected producers, consumers, and decomposers much as goods move through linked stages of production and exchange. Disruption at one node can propagate through the network and alter the viability of distant participants.
be_5 filler (biological vs economic) biological economic Gene Regulation as Taxes and Subsidies NA NA Gene regulation is like a system of taxes and subsidies: regulatory molecules raise or lower the biochemical “cost” of expressing particular genes, shifting cellular resources toward some activities and away from others. Changing these incentives can reorganize cell behavior without changing the underlying genetic inventory.
be_6 filler (biological vs economic) biological economic Natural Selection as Market Competition NA NA Natural selection is like market competition: organisms with traits better suited to local conditions leave more descendants, just as firms with better-fitting strategies tend to capture more demand. Over time, unsuccessful variants disappear while successful ones become more common.
eb_1 filler (biological vs economic) economic biological Creative Destruction as Ecological Succession NA NA Creative destruction is like ecological succession: New technologies and business models can displace established industries much as new species and ecological communities replace earlier ones after environmental change. The destruction of one economic structure simultaneously opens resources and niches for another.
eb_2 filler (biological vs economic) economic biological Economic Specialization as Cell Differentiation NA NA Economic specialization is like cell differentiation: Just as cells in a multicellular organism become specialized for tasks such as contraction, signaling, or digestion, workers and firms can specialize in particular productive functions. Specialization increases efficiency but also creates mutual dependence, because no single specialized unit can perform every function the larger system requires.
eb_3 filler (biological vs economic) economic biological Market Competition as Natural Selection NA NA Market competition is like natural selection: Firms with traits that fit consumer demand tend to survive and expand, while poorly adapted firms shrink or disappear. Profits and losses act like selective pressures, continually reshaping the population of businesses.
eb_4 filler (biological vs economic) economic biological Inflation as a Rising Metabolic Rate NA NA Inflation is like a rising metabolic rate: When money circulates faster than an economy’s capacity to produce goods and services, prices can rise just as a body generates more heat when its metabolism accelerates beyond its ability to dissipate energy. The faster circulation changes the system’s operating conditions even when its underlying physical resources have not increased proportionally.
eb_5 filler (biological vs economic) economic biological Supply-and-Demand Adjustment as Biological Homeostasis NA NA Supply-and-demand adjustment is like biological homeostasis: When a shortage pushes prices upward, producers are encouraged to supply more while consumers tend to demand less, much as biological feedback mechanisms counter deviations from an equilibrium. When a surplus appears, the feedback runs in the opposite direction.
eb_6 filler (biological vs economic) economic biological Compound Interest as Exponential Population Growth NA NA Compound interest is like exponential population growth: Just as organisms reproduce and their offspring later reproduce in turn, invested returns can generate additional returns of their own. Given enough time, repeated multiplication can make small initial quantities become very large.

Claude psych_pa Scissors / fight-or-flight psychological mechanical The fight-or-flight response is like a pair of scissors: two blades that do nothing on their own, but once the handles are squeezed they pivot shut in one committed motion, cutting cleanly and all at once rather than a little at a time.
Claude psych_pa Scissors / fight-or-flight mechanical psychological Scissors are like the fight-or-flight response: they rest open and idle until a single squeeze commits both blades to converge at once in one irreversible shearing action, after which the spring returns them to standby, ready but spent.
Claude psych_be Wheelbarrow / emotion regulation psychological mechanical Emotional regulation is like a wheelbarrow: it doesn’t make the load any lighter, it just shifts the weight onto a wheel and an axle so that the ground carries most of it and you only have to steer.

Claude psych_gh Elevator / habit formation psychological mechanical Habit formation is like an elevator: sinking the shaft costs enormous effort up front, but once it’s built a single button press carries you to the same floor every time, with no climbing and no decision.
Claude psych_gh Elevator / habit formation mechanical psychological An elevator is like habit formation: the whole multi-stage sequence collapses into one button press, so after the initial cue the machinery runs the route to completion without any further deliberate input from you.

This module runs automated data-quality checks (empty columns, SPSS filter variables, category casing, stray whitespace, numbers stored as text, problematic and colliding column names, mixed text encodings, personal information, spreadsheet formatting, and careless responding) on the extracted data files.

We examined 541 columns across 24 data files.

Issues Identified

65 file/column combinations have at least one issue.

About the personal-information flags. These are pattern matches, not confirmed disclosures, and they are tuned to over-report rather than miss something. Expect false positives:

  • Column names are matched against identifying words in English and other European languages (email, telefoonnummer, geboortedatum, …). A column called phone_number flags whether or not it holds one, and an empty or already-anonymised column flags on its name alone.
  • Values are matched against the shape of an identifier. An IP address pattern also matches a version string or a dotted numeric code; a card-number pattern requires both a real issuer prefix and a checksum, but a long numeric ID can still coincide.
  • Free text is flagged when a column holds long, mostly-distinct prose — the shape open-ended answers take. Most such columns contain no names at all.

A flag means look at this column. Where the data is already de-identified (an ip column reading Anonymized, a name column the authors emptied), no action is needed.

Careless Responding

No file could be screened for careless responding.

What this does not cover. Only 0 of 24 data files could be screened: the rest had no detectable multi-item scale block, or too few respondents. Even in a screened file, these checks only look at multi-item rating scales — the only place where a repeated or flat answer pattern is interpretable. Single questions, open text, demographics and any item outside a detected scale block are never examined. A respondent can therefore answer most of a survey carelessly and still not be flagged here, and finding nothing is not evidence that a dataset is free of careless responding.

How to make your code run on another computer

We ran your code on a clean computer, the way a reader or reviewer would. Below is each problem we found, the scripts it affects, and how to fix it. Fix them in the order given: a problem near the top can cause the ones below it.

A package could not be installed.

  • analysis_study1.R needs LexOPS.
  • analysis_study2.R needs LexOPS.
  • analysis_study4.R needs LexOPS.

LexOPS could not be installed with the current version of R, probably because it is old. Record the versions you used (in R, renv::init() writes them to a renv.lock file) and your R version. To be sure the code keeps running, provide a Docker image: a frozen copy of the whole computer setup the code needs, which you can build from rocker/r-ver at your R version.

All details of the Reproducibility Check

This module assesses whether the paper’s code could be run on its data, and — because execute = TRUE — actually ran it. We examined 14 R code files.

Execution

The code was run. Each script ran in an isolated Docker container against a throwaway copy of the repository, in the run order above, with a 300-second per-script timeout. Of 14 scripts: 10 ran without error, 0 errored, 0 timed out, 3 could not run because one of its own dependencies is unavailable, 0 did not parse, and 1 was run by another script with source(). Running against current package versions: a break can reflect version drift, which argues for pinning versions.
